Highland councillors have given the go-ahead for public consultations to be held on plans for two new short-term let control zones.

One has been proposed for Inverness and the other would cover large parts of the region including Strathpeffer, Sutherland, Wester Ross, Lochaber, Skye and Raasay.

If the zones went ahead, planning permission would be needed for any new Airbnb-style holiday accommodation.

National tenants' union Living Rent wants all parts of the Highlands to have the controls to help increase the availability of housing, but the Association of Scotland's Self Caterers opposes the zones.

More stories from the Highlands and Islands

News from the Highlands and Islands on BBC Sounds

Living Rent held a demonstration outside Highland Council's headquarters in Inverness while councillors met inside to consider the plans.

A report to Thursday's economy and infrastructure committee said the two different zones would reflect variations between urban and rural locations.

According to the report, the proposed areas have higher proportions of potential homes being used as licensed short-term lets.

Officials said there were fewer affordable properties than other parts of the region.

In Inverness city centre, more than 15% of potential homes are short-term lets while the figure is more than 27% in the Fort Augustus and Invermoriston areas.

The committee agreed public consultations should go ahead, and an amendment from Lochaber Lib Dem councillor Andrew Baxter that area committees take into account the feedback and evidence from the consultation.

Chrissie Gillies, a councillor for Eilean a' Cheò, told BBC Naidheachdan: "Underneath all of the discussions around short-term let control areas is the need for houses.

"We desperately need houses."

She added: "70% of people living and working in Skye and Raasay cannot afford the houses, even at the lower end of the market."

Highland Council has already set up a control zone in Badenoch and Strathspey and is considering rolling them out in several other areas.

Campaigners from tenants' union Living Rent have criticised the current proposal, calling for all local area committees to introduce restrictions.

The organisation claims the absence of control zones has allowed a "free for all" across the Highlands, creating a "scarcity of available housing."

The Association of Scotland's Self-Caterers said it would be a mistake to extend the policy elsewhere until there was clear and unambiguous evidence that it was working.

Chief executive Fiona Campbell warned there was a danger of unintended consequences.

She said: "This plan scapegoats responsible local businesses while doing nothing to address the real issues underlying housing challenges: be it second homes, the increasing number of economically inactive empty properties and lack of housing supply."

Wolf statue outside Inverness Town House repaired after ear-shattering incident in howling gale that blew Highland Council’s Christmas tree over

By  Alasdair Fraser 

Published: 17:07, 12 February 2026

A wolf statue standing guard outside Inverness Town House has been restored to its former glory after losing an ear in a winter storm.

The repaired wolf outside Inverness Town House still looked a little bit brassed off by events yesterday, but its bark is worse than its bite. Picture: Highland Council.

The canine figurine, one of two commissioned during the extensive renovation of the civic building, was left aurally-challenged in January after being struck by a Christmas tree in a howling gale.

Some local admirers took to social media three weeks ago fearing the popular sculpture had been vandalised, only for Highland Council to clarify that it had been victim to an unfortunate mishap.

The council enlisted local stonemasons to restore the beast to rude health.

The storm-damaged wolf statue was repaired for less than £1000.

The storm-damaged wolf statue.

A Highland Council spokeswoman confirmed: “The repairs to the wolf statue outside the Town House which recently suffered storm damage are now complete and it is restored to its original splendour.

“The pigments will lighten slightly as the repair cures and the traditional stonemasons will do a follow-up check.

“The work was carried out by MacLeod & Jerrams, traditional stonemasons based in Ross-shire, at a cost of under £1000.

“We appreciate having access to such skilled local artisans.”

The two wolves sit either side of the Town Hall main entrance.

They were originally commissioned to replace the two missing dog statues that old photographs showed perched on the Town House roof, but when those were rediscovered hidden away in a council depot, the wolves were given a different position down below.
selected_articles.summary: A wolf statue at Inverness Town House, which lost an ear after being struck by a falling Christmas tree in a January storm, has been repaired by local stonemasons for less than £1,000.
selected_articles.title: Stonemason steps in for repairs after storm-damaged ear kept wolf from the door of Inverness Town House

Highland Council bus service ‘success’ could see a Lothian Buses model adopted as passenger numbers almost double and savings of almost £2m

By  Scott Maclennan 

Published: 16:30, 12 February 2026

Highland Council bus service ‘success’ could see a Lothian Buses model adopted.

A new operating model for the Highland Council-run bus service will be developed after the first three years of operation delivered on passenger numbers and savings.

Councillors agreed that a report will be brought back in May with the principle idea being that the service becomes a so-called ‘Arm’s Length External Organisation’.

That would see it operate like Highlife Highland while Edinburgh Council’s Lothian Buses are frequently pointed to as an exemplar within transport.

In what is a rare success story for the local authority, passenger numbers almost doubled from 73,727 to 135,839 between 2023 and 2025.

Financially it is beneficial too in “cost avoidance” terms as contracts brought in-house totalled £4.2 million while the current in-house cost is £2.4 million.

Members of the economy and infrastructure committee were falling over themselves to congratulate the service on its delivery of reliable bus services.

Some reservations about it being an Inverness-centric policy were voiced with few benefits elsewhere but Ross-shire and Caithness have both benefitted from services.

This was no doubt the result of the council’s purchase of D&E coaches at the start of 2025 – we understand that the cost was between £5 million to £6 million.

But recent contract hikes by private providers saw the council’s transport bill for buses – typically for issues like school runs – rise from £17 million to £25 million.

On top of those savings the first tentative steps to renew the fleet are being made with the addition of three fully electric double deckers.

And there will be an open top double decker for D&E Coaches to provide an option for the familiar tours for visitors seen in many other cities.

The chief officer facilities and fleet management, Paul Reid, said passenger figures show how the service is keeping “urban and rural communities connected.”

He added: “Whilst the figures [financial savings] above clearly demonstrate the financial benefits in terms of cost avoidance, the business strategy (and subsequent growth) of the service has been largely reactive to circumstances where contracts have been given up by private sector operators (such for example in Caithness and Inverness).”
selected_articles.summary: Highland Council's in-house bus service saw passenger numbers nearly double from 73,727 to 135,839 between 2023 and 2025, achieving nearly £2 million in savings. Councillors are now considering transforming the service into an 'Arm's Length External Organisation', modeled after Edinburgh's successful Lothian Buses.
selected_articles.title: Highland Council bus service ‘success’ could see a Lothian Buses model adopted

Grantown court costs row: auditor’s report goes to the sheriff

Resolution of a bitter row over the legal costs concerning a Strathspey community’s battle with the Highland Council has drawn a little closer today.

Grantown Community Council stood firm against the council’s plan to charge for use of the Strathspey capital’s public square and took the issue to court.

Their fight was successful and the court awarded them costs of £20,000.

But as one local complained last week: “The intransigent Highland Council hasn’t the grace to accept the legal decision on payment of costs for losing - fairly comprehensively - the Grantown Common Good case.

“The court awarded costs of £20,000 to the community council to cover legal fees but Highland Council has challenged that decision by claiming the £7,000 that the local watchdog group raised to fight the legal case should be deducted from the costs to be paid.”

Both sides are in a legal and accounting battle to settle the matter.

SQUARE GO: The campaigners fought the charging plan from the start.

The local campaigners intend that any money left over from the case, including generous public donations, would be spent wholly on Grantown.

Campaigner Gordon Bulloch complained: “Highland Council now want to access these well-meaning donations for this money to disappear into the Highland Council coffers. I doubt that any of the donors would agree to this if asked.”

Local Highland councillors would not comment on the issue while it was still in the hands of legal advisers, although Aviemore’s Bill Lobban reminded the community that is the plan had been approved the financial position of the Common Good Fund would have been “secure for all time to come.”

This evening a Highland Council spokesperson told the Strathy: “The Court Auditor has now submitted their report to Inverness Sheriff Court and we await a response from the court."
selected_articles.summary: A court auditor has submitted a report to Inverness Sheriff Court concerning a dispute over legal costs between Grantown Community Council and Highland Council. The community council, which successfully challenged council fees for public space use, was awarded £20,000 but the council is disputing part of the payment.
selected_articles.title: Grantown court costs row: council report goes to Sheriff

Highland Council to increase roads budget by just 2.15% - despite £233 million works backlog

Inverness is set to get one of the biggest increases to its yearly allocation of the budget. Picture: James Mackenzie

Highland Council has increased the total roads budget by just 2.15 per cent despite the most recent repairs backlog figure standing at £233 million.

In papers due to be discussed by the economy and infrastructure committee on Thursday (February 12) the total roads budget for 2026/27 is £21,550,000.

That is just £400,000 more than the previous financial year while figures reported in September 2025 revealed it would cost £233 million to clear the backlog of road maintenance required across the region.

Last month Thurso and Northwest Caithness councillor Matthew Reiss (Highland Alliance) said the council would require an annual roads budget of around £32m to £35m “just to stand still”. 

He added: “Each month, on average, the roads deteriorate by another million pounds worth of repairs.”

His comments came as it was revealed more than 90 per cent of road maintenance repairs required in Caithness last year were not completed.

The budget breakdown shows £7.8 million has been set as a base budget for each year since 2024/25.

A further £12.15 million was added as “top up” to the 2026/27 budget with a further £1 million set aside for emergencies and £600,000 for additional structure funding - totalling £21,550,000 for the year.

However £250,000 from the emergency stash has already been set aside for two “significant requirements” according to the report - for work at Aird Crescent in Kirkhill and flood protection measures and outfall repair at Newtonmore.

The report also states that any over- or underspend in the budget would be carried on to the next financial year.

An area breakdown shows how the budget will be divided across the Highlands.

Inverness; Caithness; Ross and Cromarty; and Skye and Raasay will all get over £3 million each for the year.

Sutherland and Lochaber areas will be allocated just over £2 million each while Badenoch and Strathspey is allocated just under £1 million and Nairn gets £682,485.

The Inverness and Ross and Cromarty areas both saw the biggest increases from last year's allocation, with the city getting £72,236 more and Ross and Cromarty’s budget increasing by £77,108.

Members of the committee have been asked to agree to the funding allocations and specific projects at Thursday's meeting.

duplicates.summary: Highland councillors narrowly rejected a motion to formally acknowledge a £233 million roads maintenance backlog and request a meeting with the Scottish Government for more funding. The current annual roads budget of £21.55 million will stand, despite warnings it is insufficient.
duplicates.title: Highland councillors narrowly vote NOT to ask for more roads cash

selected_articles.summary: Highland Council has allocated £21.55m for roads in 2026/27, a 2.15% increase. This comes despite a maintenance backlog estimated at £233 million. The budget will be divided among regions, with Inverness and Ross and Cromarty receiving the largest increases.
selected_articles.title: Slight increase in roads budgets set against £233 million repairs backlog

Sutherland’s former Melvich police station could be set for a house conversion under plans lodged with Highland Council

By Philip Murray 

Published: 11:38, 12 February 2026

The former police house and annexe, which contained the police station, cell and garage, were recently up for sale. Plans have been submitted to turn the annexe into its own one-bedroom property.

A former police station and garage could be turned into a house after plans were lodged with Highland Council.

Applicant Malcolm Morrison has submitted a change of use application for the former Melvich police station and attached house.

The building, which has been in residential use for many years, currently features a two-storey three-bedroom house, and an attached single-storey annexe that once contained the former police station, cell room, and a garage.

If approved, the two-storey house would remain unaltered, but the police station and garage annexe would be refit to turn it into its own one-bedroom dwelling.

Drawings submitted with the application show that part of the internal garage wall and one of the cell's walls would be removed to create a larger open plan kitchen, dining and lounge area.

The existing entrance door would be blocked up and the police station reception room inside it converted into a bedroom.

An existing storage room would also be knocked through into the toilet room to create a larger shower room. Other changes would include the replacement of the existing garage door with large patio doors. An accessible path and entrance would also be created to the rear of the building.

The former police station grounds would also house a new dedicated outdoor parking space.

The proposals come after the building was put up for sale for offers over £90,000. The house and police station are currently listed as "under offer".

On their listing, through estate agent Yvonne Fitzgerald, the police station and garage is described as an annexe "which could be utilised into a further room" for the house "or would make an ideal AirBnB".

If approved, the planning application would keep the house and police station as separately accessed properties, but their intended future use is not listed.

Visit the Public Notice Portal to find out more about planning applications that affect you.
selected_articles.summary: A planning application has been submitted to Highland Council to convert the annexe of a former police station in Sutherland into a separate one-bedroom dwelling. The annexe, which previously housed the station, a cell, and a garage, would be internally reconfigured and fitted with patio doors.
selected_articles.title: Former police station annexe set for house conversion?

‘Weak’ leadership at an Inverness secondary school is hindering efforts to raise attainment among pupils in one of Scotland’s most poverty-stricken catchment areas.

A new inspectors’ report criticises the pace of change at Inverness High School and calls for better strategic planning.

The inspection findings, just published by His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Education in Scotland (HMIE), highlight positives in the standard of teaching, learning and assessment, as well as good groundwork for change set in place by senior staff including headteacher Vikki Forrester, who took the post 18 months ago.

But it also points to weaknesses in raising attainment in areas such as literacy and numeracy, as well as concerns over the school’s approach to wellbeing, equality and inclusion.

The High School, the city’s second oldest, moved into the city centre art deco building at Montague Row, west of the River Ness, in 1937.

With a recently falling school roll of just under 500 pupils, its demographic in drawing from Merkinch, Dalneigh and the city centre makes it one of Scotland’s most challenging schools.

In September 2025, almost nine out of 10 High School pupils were classed as living in the lowest fifth most deprived areas of Scotland.

Just short of a third were registered for free school meals, while three out of four had additional support needs.

Daily attendance falls below the national average and and exclusions above it, although the report adds: “This has begun to show signs of improvement and the headteacher recognises it (as) an improvement priority.”

Set against that background, the quality of teaching and learning at the High School is often masked in national school tables, with the report placing all findings in proper context.

But it also noted areas of decline or stagnation in attainment set against the High School’s own previous standards.

Describing weak ‘leadership of change’, the report states: “There is a significant need to improve strategic leadership at all levels across the school.

“Senior leaders recognise that the pace of change has not been sufficient to achieve desired improvements in the outcomes for young people.

“They should now work with staff, young people, parents and partners to significantly increase the pace of change to drive forward identified improvement priorities.

Teaching has been praised at the school in a number of areas, with plans for improvement in place but needing to gather pace, according to inspectors.

“Almost all of the identified priority improvement areas for the school remain at an early stage of development and progress.

“The headteacher and senior leaders need to review their responsibilities and apply a robust and coordinated approach to strategic leadership across all areas of the school (and) continue to look outwards to strengthen their awareness of national standards and expectations.

“This will also help to identify highly-effective practice to progress and formalise the school’s improvement work.”

The report says senior staff had a clear understanding of the priorities of Developing the Young Workforce (DYW) in supporting young people to gain the necessary skills for learning, life and the world of work.

But it adds: “There is no clear strategic vision or action plan to embed these priorities throughout the school.

“As a next step, senior leaders should work with staff and key partners to plan, review and measure progress against implementing these priorities.”

Learning, teaching and assessment at the school was judged ‘satisfactory’ in the report, with praise for staff in fostering “positive relationships with most young people”, who were mostly “respectful and compliant” in “a calm environment” for learning.

It applauded the work of a teachers’ group in drawing up guidelines to improve the consistency of lessons across the school.

The majority of teachers provided “clear instructions, explanations, and demonstrations”, but there was a need for improvement in highlighting how lessons would help in learning skills for life and work.

It adds: “Young people have limited formal opportunities to identify and reflect on their skills.

“As a next step, senior leaders should work with learners, staff and partners to develop a whole school approach to developing young people’s skills.”

Ensuring wellbeing, equality and inclusion was classed as being ‘weak’, despite a majority of young people feeling safe in school and most staff fostering “positive and caring relationships” with young people.

It adds: “Senior leaders and staff should work together to promote an inclusive and respectful environment across the wider school campus.”

It also notes that “a significant minority of young people and parents report that the school does not deal well with bullying”, with progress to be made in learning about diversity and equality.

A Highland Council spokesman said: “The local authority takes any inspection findings seriously and is working closely with the school leadership team to ensure that all necessary steps are in place to support continuous improvement.

“As the inspection notes, the headteacher at the school has been in post for 18 months, during which time she has rightly identified several key areas for improvement and has begun working with staff to drive forward change.

“The Highland Council is committed to providing quality learning environments, experiences and interactions for our pupils.

“An action plan has already been developed with the school which will continue to focus on all areas for improvement.

“This will be regularly evaluated by the school leadership team supported by senior education officers.”
selected_articles.summary: An inspection report criticizes weak strategic leadership at Inverness High School for hindering the pace of improvement. The school serves one of Scotland's most deprived catchment areas. While teaching was satisfactory, attainment in literacy and numeracy remains a concern, and bullying handling needs improvement.
selected_articles.title: ‘Weak’ leadership blamed for slow progress in raising standards at Inverness secondary school

Police are hunting two teenagers after a 94-year-old woman was pushed to the ground and robbed in a "despicable" attack in Falkirk town centre.

The woman's handbag was stolen in the incident, which happened on Hope Street at the junction with Meeks Road at about 12:55 on Monday.

Officers said the woman was badly shaken but did not require medical treatment.

Detectives said two males were seen running away from the area around the time towards Dollar Park.

Both are described as white, in their teens and of slim build.

The first was wearing black Nike trousers, a black and grey Nike jacket and Nike 95 trainers, black gloves, a black face-covering and a black crossbody bag.

The second was wearing a black Montirex jacket, black trousers, black Nike 95 trainers, black gloves, a black crossbody bag and had his face covered.

Police said CCTV inquiries were ongoing and officers were appealing for help, external from the public to identify the suspects.

Det Sgt Chris Scott said: "This is a despicable attack on an elderly woman in the town centre. 

"I'd urge anyone who recognises the descriptions or saw what happened, to come forward. 

"Anyone with private CCTV, doorbell or dash-cam footage between Hope Street to Dollar Park is asked to review this for anything which may assist our investigation.

"I would also like to appeal directly to parents or carers of youths in the area as we believe these teenagers are local."

Hillfoots win 49-12 in battle with Falkirk 2nd XV

Rugby league

Sport

This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald.

Caledonia Division 1 Midlands

Hillfoots - 47

Falkirk 2nd XV - 12

Hillfoots turned in a composed performance on Saturday to brush aside Falkirk's second string, thus taking another step towards securing a creditable third place in the division.

The early exchanges were tight, with neither team particularly impressing for the first ten minutes or so.

Gradually, playing up the hill, the home team started gaining the upper hand.

The lineout was functioning reasonably well and the scrum was once again a dominant weapon.

Strong running from Shaun Barton

Pleasingly, Foots' backline looked full of running despite the muddy conditions, with stand-off Peter Duncan pulling the strings and looking to get the dangerous back three of Ryan Butterworth, Jamie Urquhart and Grant Carmichael into positions where their pace and power would reap dividends.

Foots claimed the first try of the game when quick hands saw Urquhart beat a couple of defenders before heading infield and popping to Butterworth who dived to the line.

Urquhart added the extras and soon after converted a penalty for a 10-0 lead.

Jamie Urquhart scoring his first of the day

Further first half tries from number-eight Shaun Barton and Urquhart, neither converted, stretched the score to 20-0 as half-time approached. Falkirk managed a converted score of their own right on half-time - 20-7 as the teams sucked on their oranges.

Hillfoots were keen to press home their dominance in the second half and duly did so with four more tries, the pick of the bunch being scored by Butterworth who embarked on one of his trademark dancing, skipping runs from wide out on halfway, bamboozled half a dozen would-be Falkirk tacklers and slid under the posts Klinsmann-style for a tremendous score.

Peter Duncan looking for a gap

Scrum-half Kris Illingworth finished off a pushover try and both Urquhart brothers claimed five-pointers, Jack coming off the bench to score wide on the left with the last move of the game following Jamie’s earlier try on the opposite wing.

Jamie added a couple of conversions and another penalty which all added up to very satisfactory day at the office for the Tilly men, and for Jamie in particular who was awarded the Man of the Match jacket.

Jack Urquhart on the way to the line

There are now two free weekends due to Six Nations games.

The next fixtures are on Saturday 28th February.

The 1st XV travel to Broughty Ferry to take on Panmure and the Rams have a Spirit of Rugby game at Falkirk, both 3pm kick-offs.
selected_articles.summary: Hillfoots RFC defeated Falkirk 2nd XV 49-12 in a Caledonia Division 1 Midlands match. The dominant performance, featuring tries from players like Ryan Butterworth and Jamie Urquhart, solidifies the team's position in third place within the division.
selected_articles.title: Hillfoots RFC win 49-12 to further solidify third place in the division

Falkirk Council  

Executive to consider Digital Strategy 2026–2031

Proposals include a main online access point and more help for people who need it.

The Digital Strategy will make services easier to navigate online. 

Councillors will be asked to consider the Digital Strategy 2026-2031 at the next meeting of the Executive on 19 February. 

The proposal sets out how the Council aims to make it easier to access services online, strengthen cyber security, and offer more support for people who are not confident using digital tools. 

Easier access to services 

The strategy aims to make it easier for residents to get the help they need, whenever they need it. A major part of this programme is giving residents round the clock access to support through a smart digital assistant. 

The 24/7 tool will be able to answer everyday questions, guide people straight to the right service, and help with simple tasks without the hassle of searching through multiple pages or contact details. This will cut the effort for residents, speeding up responses, and making the experience of dealing with the Council simpler, smoother, and more convenient. 

There will also be a focus on reducing digital exclusion, so that people who struggle with devices, internet access or confidence can still get the help they need. 

This includes practical support through libraries and community locations, free community Wi-Fi, device lending, drop-in help sessions, and continued support for low-income households, including connectivity support such as SIM cards and advice on affordable broadband and social tariffs. 

Safer systems behind the scenes 

Behind the scenes, the strategy sets out plans to replace older systems and improve how internal systems work together. The aim is to reduce manual admin and speed up processes, so employees can spend more time supporting frontline services. 

It will also strengthen cyber security, including 24/7 monitoring to spot threats early and tighter controls on who can access information, making sure data is protected at every step. 

Karen Algie, Director of Transformation, Communities and Corporate Services, said:

If approved, this strategy will make it easier than ever for residents to access the services they need, strengthen how we protect information, and ensure anyone who needs extra help getting online can get it.

"It also shows how we’ll modernise the tools our employees rely on every day, so they can deliver faster, more reliable support.

"Technology should remove barriers, make it easier to get the help you need, simplify the experience, and make sure no one is left behind.
selected_articles.summary: Councillors will consider the Digital Strategy 2026-2031 on 19 February. The strategy proposes making services easier to access online, strengthening cyber security, and offering more support for residents who are not confident using digital tools.
selected_articles.title: Executive to consider Digital Strategy 2026–2031

Frox, of Falkirk - Scotland's designer boutique

Weddings

Fiona Wilson, owner of Frox of Falkirk, has dressed Scottish wedding mothers for 17 years (Image: web) 

Frox of Falkirk is Scotland’s destination boutique for Mother of the Bride & Groom and occasion wear outfits. Whether you are looking for a classic style, or something fabulous and modern, they have it all!

Frox of Falkirk is located in the heart of the central belt, only 30 minutes from Glasgow and Edinburgh, with ample transport and parking facilities.

“I love what I do!” Fiona admitted. “Weddings are such happy occasions – everyone comes in smiling, excited about the day ahead.”

Starting during the 2009 recession, Fiona transformed a Falkirk boutique into Frox of Falkirk, relaunching with her own carefully curated stock.

17 years later, she carries over 3000 garments across a wide range of designers, including Couture Club, Gabriela Sanchez, Fely Campo, Irresistible, Carla Ruiz, Gill Harvey and more. Prices range from £300 to £3000, and for those wanting something unique, Fiona can create exclusive pieces that combine elements from multiple designs. Specialising in fuller figure outfits, Frox of Falkirk stock sizes 6 to 36 in store, and bespoke outfits can also be made in bigger sizes to accommodate the customers needs.

Customer service is at the heart of the business. “You often see customers who are timid at first, and then as they find the right dress, they light up. By the end, they’re ecstatic – it’s such a joyful moment.”

Appointments are preferred, though walk-ins are welcome, with visits typically lasting around 90 minutes. Fiona and her consultants guide clients through colours, shapes and styles that complement their figures. “We recommend bringing two additional people – more than that can sometimes become overwhelming,” she said.

Frox of Falkirk caters to all weddings, from traditional church ceremonies to barns, marquees and outdoor farm celebrations.

Fiona draws on her rural background – brought up on a smallholding at Cumbernauld, with her grandfather running a farm and her father in wholesale and retail milk – giving her a keen understanding of the needs of clients from farming communities.

Alongside outfits, the shop stocks shoes, headpieces and accessories, providing a complete one-stop-shop experience. Alterations are handled by a trusted freelance seamstress.

Looking ahead, Fiona is happy to maintain her current location.

Around 100 workers have begun a formal grievance procedure with Falkirk Council after being told they need to pay for background checks, despite not working with children or vulnerable adults.

GMB Scotland says that staff in the building maintenance team at Falkirk Council have been told a change to the rules means they are now included in the Protecting Vulnerable Groups (PVG) scheme.

According to the union, around 100 of the staff affected have now signed a formal grievance claiming the vetting is unnecessary and that asking affected staff to pay the £59 cost is unfair.

Raymond Smith, GMB organiser at the council, questioned the need for staff in the building division to be vetted when they are not in regulated roles, in caring, teaching, supervising or supporting, with children or vulnerable adults.

He said there is no public safety reason for the scheme, run by Disclosure Scotland, to be extended and questioned the guidance to Falkirk Council, suggesting any tradesperson that is alone in a regulated building must be vetted.

Mr. Smith said: “Our members are not in those roles and largely carry out emergency repairs in regulated buildings or possibly empty flats in sheltered housing.

“If they need to be vetted so must every worker visiting the premises for any reason.

“Disclosure Scotland could not answer why, for example, a gas fitter from Falkirk Council visiting the building needs a PVG but a network engineer does not.”

The union has had meetings with council officials to raise workers’ concerns and urged the local authority to pay the costs of PVG vetting for workers while questioning the need for the additional checks with Disclosure Scotland.

Smith said staff with similar roles in other local authorities do not apparently require PVG checks and called for clarity on vetting guidelines.

He said: “We have no issue with all necessary vetting and background checks, but the scheme must be applied lawfully, proportionately, consistently and not a blanket approach.

“There seems little need for these workers to be vetted at all and there is certainly no justification for asking them to pay for it.

“It will achieve little apart from raising revenue for Disclosure Scotland.”

A spokesperson for Falkirk Council said: “The PVG Scheme operates Scotland-wide and ensures those working with vulnerable groups have appropriate checks in place. With national criteria setting out which posts require membership of the Scheme, it aims to reduce any risk to the most vulnerable in our communities.

“The Scheme has been in place since 2014 and was updated last year, including changes to the membership criteria. All Council posts have been assessed against this to ensure this legislation is applied appropriately. All employees in the Council pay for the cost of membership.

“Any employment issue is managed in line with our internal policies. We are unable to comment on any specific case.”

A Disclosure Scotland spokesperson also said they could not comment on individual cases.

The spokesperson said: “The Disclosure (Scotland) Act 2020 enhanced safeguarding in Scotland by making the Protecting Vulnerable Groups scheme (the PVG scheme) a legal requirement for anyone carrying out a regulated role. The Protection of Vulnerable Groups (Scotland) Act 2007 sets out the criteria for a regulated role.”

“Individuals and organisations should review the legislative criteria to determine if they are carrying out, or offering, a regulated role. Disclosure Scotland have published guidance, and provide training and advice, to help individuals and organisations to determine if a job is a regulated role.

“It is a criminal offence to require a PVG scheme disclosure for a role that is not a regulated role.”
selected_articles.summary: Around 100 Falkirk Council building maintenance staff have begun a formal grievance after being told they must pay £59 for background checks. Their union argues the checks are unnecessary as they do not work with children or vulnerable adults, calling the mandate unfair.
selected_articles.title: Outrage after 100 council workers told to pay for own background checks

Volcano Watch — Handling the pressure: what gases trapped inside crystals tell us

February 12, 2026, 5:00 PM HST

Volcano Watch is a weekly article and activity update written by US Geological Survey Hawaiian Volcano Observatory scientists and affiliates. This week’s article was written by HVO post-doc researcher Heather Winslow.

Image of an olivine crystal taken with a petrographic microscope. A) Olivine with melt inclusion (honey color) with a vapor gas bubble inside it (black circle). B) Zoomed in view of olivine highlighting a fluid inclusion (black circle, white dot in center) and a melt inclusion. USGS images.

Volcanic gases can give us critical information in the lead up to a hazardous eruption. USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory scientists use permanent and portable gas monitoring stations to measure gas concentrations and emission rates above the surface of our volcanoes. But, to look at gases below the surface we turn to petrologists (a scientist who studies the origins of rocks and minerals), who can find gases trapped within volcanic rocks.

Gases within volcanic rocks can be measured to estimate gas compositions and magma storage depths before the lava erupted on the surface. In geology, we refer to gases below the surface as volatiles, referring to the elemental composition of the gas, which can be a solid, liquid, or vapor phase. When referred to as a gas, it means a volatile has transitioned into the vapor phase. The most common gases (or vapor phase volatiles) emitted at the surface are water (H2O), carbon dioxide (CO2), and sulfur dioxide (SO2).

But how can we measure volatiles that are trapped within the magma before it erupts? By analyzing tiny droplets that become trapped within crystals such as olivine. These tiny droplets, called inclusions, can contain different materials. Melt inclusions contain the magma (in solid form), while fluid inclusions can contain drops of water (H2O), carbon dioxide (CO2), and sulfur dioxide (SO2) in the liquid or gas phase.

Once an inclusion has been trapped, the surrounding crystal acts as a pressure-capsule and retains information about the magma at the time the inclusion was formed.

In volcanoes, fluid inclusions are dominantly composed of CO2. At magmatic temperatures (1200˚ C or 2192˚ F), the density of the CO2 strongly depends on pressure, which is influenced by the depth of the magma at that point in time.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW AD

Thus, if we can measure the density of the CO2 within a fluid inclusion, we can estimate the pressure at which that fluid inclusion was trapped in the growing crystal and infer the depth under the volcano where the magma was when that crystal grew. Determining storage depths of crystals has large implications for how we understand volcanoes and how shallow or deep magmas reside below the surface before they rise to erupt.

Fluid inclusion density is measured by creating thin slices of the crystals that are analyzed using Raman Spectroscopy. One challenge in this process, however, is that fluid inclusions are so very tiny they can be hard to identify! They can range in size from approximately 0.01–0.1 mm (0.0004–0.004 inches) in diameter.

University of Hawaiʻi at Hilo undergraduates using the petrographic microscope to identify fluid inclusions within olivine crystals. USGS photo.

In 2025, HVO scientists conducted and participated in a short workshop on fluid inclusion sample preparation and identification at the University of Hawaiʻi, Hilo for undergraduate students and professors.

During the workshop, UHH students and staff learned laboratory techniques for identifying fluid inclusions and how to properly prepare the crystals for Raman Spectroscopy. This process is a recently developed method and results for magma storage depths can be attained very quickly after sample collection.

An undergraduate student in the UHH Geology Department helped initiate the fluid inclusion workshop because of their research interests in using this technique to estimate the depth magma was stored before recent Kīlauea eruptions.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW AD

The collaborative relationship between HVO and the UHH Geology Department has been strengthened over the years thanks to the cooperative agreement established in 1998. Through the agreement, UHH undergraduate students participate in eruption response and apply what they learn in the classroom directly to impactful work with HVO.

During each new eruption at Kīlauea, this technique provides another important tool for HVO scientists to understand hazards in Hawaii’s frequent eruptions. Preliminary results from episodes that span from mid-January 2025 to early July 2025 show that the magmas came from about 1 mile (1.5 km) deep beneath the surface, which is the location of the shallow Halema’uma’u magma chamber.

Volcano Activity Updates

Kīlauea has been erupting episodically within the summit caldera since Dec. 23, 2024. Its USGS Volcano Alert level is WATCH.

Episode 41 lava fountaining happened for just over 8 hours on Jan. 24. Summit region inflation since the end of episode 41 indicates that another fountaining episode is possible and could occur between Feb. 13 and 17 and is most likely between Feb. 14 and 16. No unusual activity has been noted along Kīlauea’s East Rift Zone or Southwest Rift Zone.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW AD

Maunaloa is not erupting. Its USGS Volcano Alert Level is at NORMAL.

Two earthquakes were reported felt in the Hawaiian Islands during the past week: a M3.1 earthquake 10 km (6 mi) E of Pāhala at 30 km (18 mi) depth on Feb. 7 at 5:59 p.m. HST and a M3.1 earthquake 8 km (4 mi) N of Hala‘ula at 39 km (24 mi) depth on Feb. 7 at 3:36 a.m. HST.

HVO continues to closely monitor Kīlauea and Maunaloa.

Visit HVO’s website for past Volcano Watch articles, Kīlauea and Maunaloa updates, volcano photos, maps, recent earthquake information, and more. Email questions to askHVO@usgs.gov.
selected_articles.summary: USGS and University of Hawaiʻi scientists analyze microscopic gas bubbles, called fluid inclusions, trapped in olivine crystals. Measuring the density of carbon dioxide in these inclusions helps estimate magma storage pressures and depths—about one mile deep for recent Kīlauea eruptions.
selected_articles.title: Volcano Watch — Handling the pressure: what gases trapped inside crystals tell us

MOL, SINOPEC and Marubeni sign MoU on marine biodiesel supply

Mitsui OSK Lines Ltd (MOL), China’s largest fuel supplier SINOPEC Zhejiang Zhoushan Petroleum and Japan’s Marubeni Corporation have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to establish a long-term supply system for marine biodiesel fuel.  
The agreement was announced in December and marks a collaborative step to support wider adoption of lower-carbon fuels in the maritime sector.  
Under the terms of the MoU, MOL will promote the use of biodiesel fuel in marine transport, particularly in China, while SINOPEC and Marubeni will develop vital infrastructure.  
This includes storage, transportation facilities and supply ports to ensure a stable and continuous supply of biodiesel fuel to shipowners and operators.  
The shipping industry is under increasing pressure from regulators and customers alike to lower greenhouse gas emissions, and biodiesel is seen as one practical solution in the transition toward decarbonisation.  
MOL sees China as a key source of biodiesel feedstocks and aims to establish an early framework for procurement and supply in partnership with SINOPEC and Marubeni.  
The agreement supports MOL’s broader environmental strategy under its “BLUE ACTION 2035” management plan, which targets net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.  
The MoU is described by MOL as an important milestone in expanding the use of low-carbon fuels and reducing carbon emissions across global marine transport.

MOL will promote biodiesel use in shipping, while SINOPEC and Marubeni will develop related infrastructure in China to support decarbonization in maritime transport.

The Biodiesel Price Index plays a critical role in tracking global Biodiesel Prices and understanding fuel cost movements across major regions. This Biodiesel Price Trend Analysis explores recent price movements, historical data, index insights, and the Biodiesel future price outlook for the next 12 months.  

Biodiesel Current Price Movements:  

Recent Biodiesel Prices have shown moderate volatility across key producing and consuming regions including Europe, North America, South America, and Asia. Market fluctuations are largely driven by feedstock cost variations, renewable fuel mandates, and broader energy market movements.  

In late 2025, several regions witnessed firm pricing due to tightening vegetable oil supplies and strong blending mandates. However, certain Asian markets experienced temporary corrections supported by improved logistics and seasonal production increases. Overall, the Biodiesel price today reflects a market balancing regulatory demand and raw material cost pressure.

North America maintains relatively stable pricing supported by renewable fuel standards. Meanwhile, South America and Asia show competitive pricing structures influenced by feedstock availability and export activity.  

This snapshot indicates that Biodiesel Prices are not uniform globally. Instead, they reflect regional policy frameworks, supply chain conditions, and demand strength.  

Biodiesel Price Trend Analysis:  

A detailed Biodiesel Price Trend Analysis shows that prices have remained structurally supported over the past year. The long-term trend indicates resilience due to  
• Expanding renewable energy mandates  
• Growing decarbonization initiatives  
• Increasing biofuel blending targets  
• Energy market correlations  

Short-term volatility continues to emerge from feedstock market swings, particularly soybean oil, palm oil, and used cooking oil markets. When feedstock prices rise, the Biodiesel price index typically follows upward. Conversely, improved crop output or supply chain normalization may ease pressure.  
Overall, the broader Biodiesel Prices trend remains moderately bullish with periodic corrections.  

Biodiesel Price Chart & Index - What It Suggests:  

The Biodiesel price chart provides visual clarity on monthly and quarterly price movements. By analyzing the Biodiesel price index, stakeholders can identify  
• Seasonal demand spikes

• Feedstock-driven price surges  
• Energy-linked pricing correlations

For procurement teams and investors, tracking the Biodiesel price chart allows better budgeting and hedging decisions.  

Biodiesel Price Historical Analysis Data:  

Examining Biodiesel price history reveals cyclical pricing behavior influenced by agricultural output, crude oil fluctuations, and government mandates.   

Historically, price spikes align with  
• Feedstock shortages  
• Export restrictions  
• High crude oil prices  
• Increased renewable blending requirements  

Meanwhile, price corrections generally follow improved harvest seasons or reduced energy costs. This historical perspective helps interpret current Biodiesel Prices within a broader market cycle rather than viewing fluctuations as isolated events.  

Understanding Biodiesel price history is essential for forecasting long-term procurement strategies.  

Factors Driving Recent Biodiesel Price Trend Increases:  

Several core factors are contributing to recent increases in the price of Biodiesel  
1. Feedstock Cost Inflation: Vegetable oils remain the largest cost component in biodiesel production. Rising agricultural prices directly influence Biodiesel Prices.  
2. Renewable Fuel Mandates: Stronger sustainability targets across Europe and North America are increasing structural demand.  
3. Energy Market Linkages: Higher fossil fuel prices improve biodiesel competitiveness, pushing demand upward.  
4. Logistics and Freight Costs: Shipping volatility and transportation expenses add cost pressure in export-oriented markets.  
5. Carbon Compliance Costs: Environmental certification and sustainability compliance add additional operational costs.  

These combined drivers continue shaping the Biodiesel Price Trend Analysis in 2026.  

Biodiesel Price Forecast Next 12 Months:

• Stable renewable blending targets

• Global energy transition momentum

Stakeholders should closely monitor feedstock crop forecasts and crude oil movements for early signals of price shifts.  

Regional Price Differences for Biodiesel:

• Weather-related crop updates

• Freight rate changes

Palm Oil Prices Slide Again As Rival Oils Stay Weak

Malaysia kept export duty at 9%, but softer biodiesel plans and expectations of higher output are weighing on futures even as a weaker ringgit offers some demand support.

Palm oil futures in Malaysia are falling again, set for a second straight weekly drop as competing vegetable oils stay soft and expectations for rising supply build.

Benchmark palm oil is moving with the wider edible-oils complex – when soybean or rapeseed oil gets cheaper, buyers can switch, pulling palm along for the ride. Malaysia’s export duty stayed at 9% even after the March reference price rose, so policy tweaks aren’t the big story this week. Instead, the market’s focused on two forces: Indonesia putting the brakes on biodiesel expansion, which could cap demand growth, and seasonal production picking up in the months ahead. A slightly weaker ringgit offers some cushion by making exports cheaper in dollar terms, but it hasn’t been enough to flip sentiment.

Why should I care?

**For markets:** Vegetable oils tend to trade in a bundle.

Palm oil rarely trades solo – weakness in China’s Dalian contracts or US soybean oil can drag it lower even without fresh Malaysia-specific news. The key question is whether Indonesia’s biodiesel pause is temporary or a longer cooling of policy-driven demand. If supply rises as expected, prices may keep probing support levels until physical buyers step in more aggressively.

**The bigger picture:** Indonesia’s choices ripple through food and fuel.

As the world’s top producer, Indonesia can shift global pricing through planting, export rules, and biofuel mandates. Early signals of continued planting suggest supply could keep growing into 2025, even as biodiesel ambitions look less certain. More output without the same demand tailwind would ease pressure on food inflation, but it could squeeze growers and producers if prices stay capped.
selected_articles.summary: Malaysian palm oil futures fell for a second consecutive week, pressured by softness in competing vegetable oils, Indonesia's pause on biodiesel expansion, and expectations of rising seasonal production. A weaker ringgit provided only limited support for export demand.
selected_articles.title: Palm Oil Prices Slide Again As Rival Oils Stay Weak

Asia - Biodiesel - Market Analysis, Forecast, Size, Trends And Insights

IndexBox has just published a new report: Asia - Biodiesel - Market Analysis, Forecast, Size, Trends And Insights.

This article provides a comprehensive analysis of the biodiesel market in Asia for 2024, with forecasts to 2035. It details that the market volume reached 14 million tons in 2024, with a value of $15.2 billion, and is projected to grow to 21 million tons ($33.7 billion) by 2035, representing a CAGR of +3.7% in volume and +7.5% in value. Indonesia dominates both consumption (64%) and production (57%). The region is a net exporter, with China being the largest exporter, while imports saw a significant decline in 2024. The report also covers per capita consumption, import/export prices, and the performance of other key countries like Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore.

Key Findings

Asia's biodiesel market is forecast to reach 21M tons ($33.7B) by 2035, growing at a CAGR of +3.7% in volume and +7.5% in value
Indonesia is the dominant market leader, accounting for approximately 64% of total consumption and 57% of production in 2024
The region is a net exporter, with China being the largest exporter by volume, while imports fell sharply by -53.6% in 2024
Singapore has the highest per capita biodiesel consumption in Asia at 115 kg per person
Market prices showed volatility, with import prices declining to $893 per ton and export prices to $1,069 per ton in 2024

Market Forecast

Driven by increasing demand for biodiesel in Asia, the market is expected to continue an upward consumption trend over the next decade. Market performance is forecast to decelerate, expanding with an anticipated CAGR of +3.7% for the period from 2024 to 2035, which is projected to bring the market volume to 21M tons by the end of 2035.

In value terms, the market is forecast to increase with an anticipated CAGR of +7.5% for the period from 2024 to 2035, which is projected to bring the market value to $33.7B (in nominal wholesale prices) by the end of 2035.

Consumption

Asia's Consumption of Biodiesel

After three years of growth, consumption of biodiesel decreased by -0.9% to 14M tons in 2024. In general, consumption, however, continues to indicate strong growth. The volume of consumption peaked at 14M tons in 2023, and then contracted slightly in the following year.

The value of the biodiesel market in Asia dropped to $15.2B in 2024, approximately equating the previous year. This figure reflects the total revenues of producers and importers (excluding logistics costs, retail marketing costs, and retailers' margins, which will be included in the final consumer price). Overall, consumption, however, showed a prominent expansion. Over the period under review, the market hit record highs at $15.3B in 2023, and then contracted in the following year.

Consumption By Country

The country with the largest volume of biodiesel consumption was Indonesia (9M tons), comprising approximately 64% of total volume. Moreover, biodiesel consumption in Indonesia exceeded the figures recorded by the second-largest consumer, Thailand (2M tons), fourfold. The third position was taken by Malaysia (698K tons), with a 4.9% share.

In Indonesia, biodiesel consumption expanded at an average annual rate of +24.4% over the period from 2013-2024. In the other countries, the average annual rates were as follows: Thailand (+7.4%) and Malaysia (+2.2%).

In value terms, Indonesia ($8.3B) led the market. The second position was held by Thailand ($3.6B). It was followed by Malaysia.

From 2013 to 2024, the average annual growth rate of value in Indonesia amounted to +25.4%. The remaining countries recorded the following: Thailand (+3.4%) and Malaysia (+3.3%).

In 2024, the highest levels of biodiesel per capita consumption were registered in Singapore (115 kg per person), followed by Indonesia (32 kg), Thailand (29 kg), and Malaysia (21 kg), while the world average was estimated at 3 kg per person.

In Singapore, biodiesel per capita consumption remained relatively stable from 2013-2024. The remaining countries showed significant growth rates: Indonesia (+23.0% annually) and Thailand (+7.1% annually).

Production

Asia's Production of Biodiesel

In 2024, production of biodiesel decreased by -5.4% to 16M tons, ending a three-year rising trend. The most prominent growth was recorded in 2016 with a 46% increase. Production peaked at 17M tons in 2023, then declined.

In value terms, biodiesel production fell to $17.3B in 2024 estimated at export prices. Despite the recent decline, overall production continues to grow when considering long-term trends. The highest point was in 2022 at $18.6B.

Production By Country

Indonesia remained the largest producer with 9.2M tons (57% share), exceeding the second-largest, Thailand (2.1M tons), fourfold. China produced 1.7M tons (11%). Indonesia experienced an annual growth rate of +12.5% from 2013-2024; Thailand grew at +7.7%, China at +5.8%.

Imports

Asia's Imports of Biodiesel

In 2024, imports decreased sharply by -53.6% to 244K tons, ending a two-year increase. The peak was 1.5M tons in 2014. In value, imports dropped to $218M in 2024, with the import peak at $903M in 2014. The most rapid growth occurred in 2018, with a 621% increase.

Imports by Country

Malaysia was the main importer, with 146K tons (~60% of total imports), followed by Singapore (34K tons, 14%), South Korea (11%), and China (5.1%). Other importers include Hong Kong SAR, Philippines, and Cyprus.

Import price in 2024 was $893/ton, down -12.5% from the previous year. Significant variation existed: Cyprus had the highest at $1,607/ton, South Korea the lowest at $744/ton.

Exports

Asia's Exports of Biodiesel

In 2024, exports declined by -31.8% to 2.3M tons after two years of growth, peaking at 3.4M tons in 2023. Export value fell to $2.4B from previous highs of $4.8B in 2022. The fastest growth in export value was in 2018 (+225%).

Major export countries included China (1.1M tons, 49%), Malaysia (688K tons, 30%), Indonesia (8.5%), and South Korea (6.4%). China’s exports grew at a CAGR of +139.4% over the period; value at $1.2B, Malaysia at $701M, Indonesia at $186M.

Export prices in 2024 stood at $1,069/ton, down -8.1% from 2023. Variations among countries: South Korea ($1,201/ton), Thailand ($1,065/ton), Indonesia ($954/ton), Malaysia ($1,019/ton). The growth rate for export prices averaged +1.9% annually from 2012-2024, peaking at $1,533/ton in 2022, then declining.

This report provides a comprehensive view of the biodiesel industry in Asia, tracking demand, supply, and trade flows across the regional value chain. It explains how demand across key channels and end-use segments shapes consumption patterns, while also mapping the role of input availability, production efficiency, and regulatory standards on supply.

Beyond headline metrics, the study benchmarks prices, margins, and trade routes so you can see where value is created and how it moves between exporters and importers within Asia. The analysis is designed to support strategic planning, market entry, portfolio prioritization, and risk management in the biodiesel landscape in Asia.
selected_articles.summary: Asia's biodiesel market is forecast to grow at a CAGR of 7.5% in value to reach $33.7 billion by 2035, according to a new IndexBox report. Indonesia dominated consumption and production in 2024, while imports fell sharply and China was the largest exporter.

The Ontario, Canada government has issued new regulations imposing a provincial biodiesel mandate that came into force April 1.

In its initial December 2013 proposal, the Ontario Ministry of the Environment called for an annual average of 2% biofuel content in all diesel fuel sold in the province from April 2014 through December 2015, followed by an annual average of biofuel content of 4% biodiesel starting after 2016.

The published regulation delays full implementation by one year, but includes a 3% intermediary phase before the 4% mandate begins in 2017.

Northern Ontario will not be included in the mandate until 2017.

The Ontario Trucking Association says it is concerned the new rules will lead to the use of biodiesel with a higher biofuel content than that currently accepted by most heavy truck engine manufacturers’ warranties.

“With the introduction of the regulations we have no choice but to see what happens,” says OTA president David Bradley. “It’s unfortunate that the legitimate concerns of the consumer were not more explicitly addressed when the Ministry of the Environment had the chance to do so during the writing of the regulation. However, going forward, we’re calling upon the Ministry of the Environment to now work with us and the Ministry of Transportation to ensure that warranty issues, fuel quality and winter performance are monitored and corrective action taken when necessary.”
selected_articles.summary: The Ontario government has issued new regulations for a provincial biodiesel mandate, requiring 2% biofuel content in diesel, rising to 4% by 2017. The trucking association is concerned the rules will exceed engine warranty limits and affect fuel quality.
selected_articles.title: Ontario Issues Biodiesel Mandates

NASA loading liquid hydrogen aboard Artemis 2 rocket in unannounced test

February 12, 2026 Steven Young

Base of the Space Launch System (SLS) rocket where the tail service masts feed propellants into the rocket’s core stage. Image: Michael Cain/Spaceflight Now.

NASA is loading liquid hydrogen aboard its Space Launch System moon rocket at the Kennedy Space Center on Thursday for an unpublicized but crucial test of the repairs made to a leaky umbilical that derailed a countdown rehearsal on Feb. 2.

The operation to load liquid hydrogen into the huge fuel tank on the rocket’s core stage was thought to be already underway at launch complex 39B on Thursday morning. The test will determine if new seals installed in the launch pad umbilical are working.

“As part of our work to assess the repair we made in the area where we saw elevated hydrogen gas concentrations during the previous wet dress rehearsal, engineers are testing the new seals by running some liquid hydrogen across the interface and partially filling the core stage liquid hydrogen tank. The data will inform the timeline for our next wet dress rehearsal,” a NASA spokesperson said about the previously unannounced test.

During the Wet Dress Rehearsal or WDR, the launch team managed hydrogen leaks from the umbilical at the base of the rocket that feeds the propellant into the rocket by stopping and starting the process, allowing the umbilical seals to warm and plug the leaks.

Liquid hydrogen is notoriously difficult to handle because its tiny molecules can escape through even the smallest imperfection in the propellant system. It is also extremely explosive when mixed with air.

The launch team was able to fully load the propellant tanks during the Feb. 2 fueling test but called off the countdown because of a large spike in hydrogen leakage when the fuel tank was pressurized during the final minutes of the countdown.

The spokesperson did not immediately provide any additional details, including the amount of hydrogen to be loaded aboard the rocket or if the propellant tank would be pressurized to duplicate the conditions that interrupted the WDR.

Following the Feb. 2 dress rehearsal, technicians disconnected the hydrogen lines which are located on a plate that retracts into a three-story-high structure that rises from the deck of the mobile launcher. There are two tail service masts, one for liquid hydrogen and one for liquid oxygen. Engineers removed and replaced the seals on two hydrogen lines.

If all goes well with the hydrogen testing on Thursday, NASA could schedule a second Wet Dress Rehearsal as soon as next week.
selected_articles.summary: NASA is testing newly installed seals on the SLS rocket's hydrogen umbilical at Kennedy Space Center. The test, involving partial liquid hydrogen loading, follows a leak that disrupted a previous rehearsal. Results will inform the schedule for the next full countdown dress rehearsal.
selected_articles.title: NASA loading liquid hydrogen aboard Artemis 2 rocket in unannounced test

Electrolysis uses electric current through a cathode and an anode to split water into its hydrogen and oxygen components, allowing the hydrogen to be captured and used as a clean energy source. During this process, little bubbles of hydrogen often stick to the cathode, wiggling and jiggling until they break away.

The micron-scale hydrogen bubbles cause a major problem, however. When they remain on the cathode, they reduce the surface area available for electrochemical reactions and increase the resistance of the system, diminishing its overall efficiency. To mitigate this issue, Duan et al. studied the electrochemistry, fluid physics, and interfacial science of the hydrogen bubble dynamics.

“These effects give rise to substantial additional overpotentials, resulting in a diminished overall energy efficiency of the electrolysis system,” said author Qiang Xu. “Therefore, gaining a comprehensive understanding of bubble evolution and conducting in-depth investigations into bubble evolution and movement are essential for the optimization of water electrolysis techniques.”

The researchers carefully tuned the voltages applied to an electrolysis system and used cameras to monitor the bubbles’ behavior. They found a critical time that determines whether the bubble will stick around and oscillate before being released, which depends on the voltage, electrolyte concentration, and the bubble’s radius. If the bubble’s evolution period — how long it takes to grow — is longer than this critical time, it oscillates.

The authors hope their work determining hydrogen bubble oscillation parameters will lead to a wider focus on the microscale phenomena involved in energy conversion processes, “where seemingly minute bubbles may represent a critical leverage point for advancing high-efficiency hydrogen production systems,” said Xu.

Source: “Dynamics of hydrogen bubble movement and oscillation on platinum microelectrodes during water electrolysis,” by Zeyuan Duan, Xuanxiang Zhao, Jinfeng Li, Yonglu She, Liejin Guo, and Qiang Xu, Applied Physics Letters (2026). The article can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0314697 .
selected_articles.summary: Scientists studied how hydrogen bubbles stick and oscillate on cathodes during water electrolysis, reducing system efficiency. They determined a critical time that predicts oscillation based on voltage, electrolyte concentration, and bubble radius, which could help optimize hydrogen production.
selected_articles.title: Will they wiggle? Determining hydrogen bubble movements during water electrolysis

This study, based on a donor co-doping strategy to improve proton-conducting efficiency, could unlock their use in upcoming clean energy technologies involving hydrogen. A newly developed ceramic material shows record-high proton conductivity at intermediate temperatures while remaining chemically stable, report researchers from Japan. Efficient hydrogen-to-electricity conversion is critical for hydrogen-based clean energy technologies, but few materials combine chemical stability with efficient proton conductivity. Thanks to an innovative donor co-doping strategy, the proposed ceramic material features increased proton concentration and mobility, realizing exceptional conductivity and stability under CO2, O2, and H2 environments.

Hydrogen is widely regarded as a key pillar of future clean energy systems because it offers a way to store energy and generate electricity without carbon emissions. To achieve this vision, technologies that can efficiently convert hydrogen into electricity and vice versa, such as fuel cells and electrolyzers, are fundamental. In this context, protonic ceramic fuel cells have attracted attention as promising solutions, owing to their lower operating temperature compared to conventional solid oxide fuel cell systems, as well as their high theoretical efficiency.

The Norby gap and proton trapping

Despite extensive research efforts, no ceramic material has demonstrated both efficient proton conductivity and long-term chemical stability at intermediate temperatures (200−400 °C) simultaneously—a problem known as the "Norby gap." The challenge lies in how protons move through solid materials. Many ceramic proton conductors rely on acceptor doping, creating oxygen vacancies, enabling the hydration that forms protons.

Credit: Angewandte Chemie International Edition (2026). DOI: 10.1002/anie.202521773

Although this strategy is effective in increasing proton concentration, it often gives rise to a phenomenon called "proton trapping," whereby protons are trapped near dopant atoms rather than moving freely through the lattice. This trapping increases the energy barrier required for proton migration and sharply reduces proton conductivity at intermediate temperatures.

Fortunately, a research team led by Professor Masatomo Yashima from the Department of Chemistry at Institute of Science Tokyo (Science Tokyo), Japan, has now presented a compelling solution. A study published online in the journal Angewandte Chemie International Edition on January 19, 2026, reports the discovery of a novel ceramic material that breaks long-standing performance limits for proton conductors. Rather than using the conventional strategy of acceptor doping, the team explored a less-studied donor co-doping strategy. The proposed approach involved introducing two donor elements—molybdenum and tungsten—into an oxygen-deficient mother material BaScO2.5.

 How the new material was tested

The researchers used solid-state synthesis and an extensive repertoire of analytical techniques, including electrical measurements, neutron diffraction, and computer simulations, to systematically study the effects of this dual-donor co-doping design on proton transport. They found that the perovskite-type oxide BaSc0.8Mo0.1W0.1O2.8 exhibited superprotonic conductivity, reaching 0.01 S/cm at 193 °C and 0.10 S/cm at 330 °C.

"These conductivity values substantially exceed those of conventional ceramic materials in this temperature region," Yashima highlights.

Why donor co-doping is a breakthrough

Further analysis revealed that this performance comes from a combination of factors. The mother material BaScO2.5 contains a large number of oxygen vacancies that enable full hydration, leading to a very high concentration of mobile protons. At the same time, donor co-doping suppresses proton trapping by lowering the activation energy, allowing protons to move easily through the crystal lattice in three dimensions. Notably, the researchers also demonstrated that BaSc0.8Mo0.1W0.1O2.8 was chemically stable in CO2, O2, and H2 environments, highlighting its potential for practical applications.

 Implications for hydrogen technologies

By showing that donor co-doping can overcome fundamental limits in proton conductivity, this study opens a new path toward cleaner, more efficient hydrogen energy systems.

"Our findings provide a powerful new design principle for realizing solid electrolytes that operate with high efficiency at intermediate temperatures. We expect this breakthrough to accelerate the practical development of next-generation protonic ceramic fuel cells, steam electrolysis cells, and other hydrogen-related energy technologies aimed at achieving a carbon-neutral society," concludes Yashima.

More information: Kensei Umeda et al, Superprotonic Conduction in Donor Co‐Doped Perovskites, Angewandte Chemie International Edition (2026). DOI: 10.1002/anie.202521773
selected_articles.summary: Researchers developed a perovskite ceramic material (BaSc0.8Mo0.1W0.1O2.8) that shows record-high proton conductivity and chemical stability at intermediate temperatures. This breakthrough overcomes the 'Norby gap' and could accelerate the development of more efficient hydrogen fuel cells and electrolyzers.
selected_articles.title: A key barrier in protonic ceramics may be fading, and hydrogen tech could benefit

Heven AeroTech Extends DoW HyTEC Work With New Contract For Hydrogen Generation Trailer

---

News provided by

Heven AeroTech

Feb 11, 2026, 08:31 ET

Share this article

STERLING, Va., Feb. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Zepher Flight Labs, a subsidiary of Heven AeroTech, a U.S.-based pioneer of hydrogen-powered, long-endurance unmanned aerial systems (UAS), has been awarded a contract modification under the Department of War's (DoW) Hydrogen at the Tactical Edge of Contested Logistics (HyTEC) program. The award supports continued development of the HyTEC hydrogen generation trailer, advancing the system toward field-ready prototyping, demonstrations, and operational evaluation.

"This effort is about taking deployable hydrogen out of the lab and into real operating environments," said Michael Buscher, president of U.S. operations at Heven AeroTech. "We're focused on delivering a system that units can rely on when fuel access is constrained, and endurance directly affects mission success."

Under the agreement, the team will collaborate with H3 Dynamics to refine the design, including expanded solar capacity to increase off-grid hydrogen production, improved mobility, and a more intuitive user experience, build a next-generation prototype, and support government demonstrations to validate performance, reliability, and deployability in austere and contested conditions. The system is designed to provide organic hydrogen generation, supporting unmanned systems, small-unit equipment, high-altitude balloons, and other mission-critical energy needs without reliance on extended fuel convoys.

"Logistics risk is a real operational constraint, not an abstract problem," said Bentzion Levinson, founder and CEO of Heven AeroTech. "HyTEC allows us to work directly with the Department to mature energy systems designed from the outset to operate independently at the tactical edge."

The HyTEC program is led by the Defense Innovation Unit, a DoW field activity tasked with accelerating the adoption of commercial technology into the military. HyTEC is focused on expanding self-sustaining energy capabilities for defense operations. Work under the current award will continue through prototype refinement, government-led demonstrations, and evaluation activities.

About Heven AeroTech  
Founded in 2019, Heven AeroTech is the market leader in hydrogen-powered, runway-independent drones engineered for mission-critical operations. Headquartered in Sterling, Virginia, Heven AeroTech designs, manufactures, and deploys unmanned systems that combine endurance, stealth, and modularity for defense, commercial, and humanitarian use. Heven AeroTech's core systems are designed and built in the U.S., with global production and operational deployments worldwide.

The Hydrogen Technology User Centre (WTAZ) has been launched in Pfeffenhausen, Bavaria. According to a report from Hydrogen Central, the project is being realized by the Technische Hochschule Ingolstadt (THI) together with HyTACC, HyTACC CRYO, the Ostbayerische Technische Hochschule Regensburg, Landshut University of Applied Sciences, the municipal company H2LA, and the Free State of Bavaria. Its aim is to establish an internationally visible infrastructure for developing and testing hydrogen-based mobility technologies.

Project Details and Funding

Federal funding of 54 million euros from federal funds and a European development programme forms the basis for the centre. Approximately 32 million euros of this will go toward the scientific infrastructure of the participating universities. The funding decisions were handed over by Federal Transport Minister Patrick Schnieder, Minister President Markus Söder, and State Minister Hubert Aiwanger.

Minister Schnieder stated that Germany is an international leader in hydrogen technology and that the centre provides an efficient innovation space to move the technology from research to application. Minister President Söder described the project as a strong signal for future mobility that strengthens Bavaria's energy and research strategy. Minister Aiwanger noted the funding allows for the setup of basic infrastructure and testing facilities, which will benefit small and medium-sized companies during the transformation toward green hydrogen mobility.

Research Roles and Infrastructure

Within the alliance, THI is taking a leading role by building a complete vehicle test bench for hydrogen-based commercial vehicles, featuring a climate chamber and simulators. The Ostbayerische Technische Hochschule Regensburg is constructing a test stand for H2 combustion engines, while Landshut University of Applied Sciences is building a thermal test stand for hydrogen storage systems. HyTACC CRYO is planning a direct liquefier for producing green liquid hydrogen, and H2LA is developing the site infrastructure.

A joint test hall with outdoor areas will be available for all partners, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises and start-ups. An existing electrolyser at the site will supply green hydrogen, creating a fully sustainable test infrastructure. Professor Hans-Joachim Hof of THI said the funding strengthens their research centre and expands its profile with the forward-looking topic of hydrogen for commercial vehicles.

The high-performance research hub is part of the National Hydrogen Innovation and Technology Centre and is planned for commissioning by the end of 2027.
